context_blurb:
Stand on a skateboard and shove a wall, and you roll away from it, as if the wall had shoved you back. It did. A force is a push or a pull, and every force has a partner: whenever one thing pushes on another, it gets pushed back. That rule explains swimming, rockets and the bug squashed on a windshield.

Isaac Newton wrote the rule down in 1687 as his third law of motion: when one object pushes or pulls on a second, the second pushes or pulls back on the first, just as hard and the opposite way. A pair is always the same two objects acting on each other. When a hammer pounds a nail, the partner of its push down on the nail is the nail's push up on the hammer. The board pushes on the nail as well, but that push belongs to another pair, between the nail and the board.

The two forces of a pair begin together, too: a girl leaning on a heavy door feels it press back on her hands from the moment she starts to push on it, however gently, before it has moved at all. The word "reaction" makes the second push sound like a later reply, but neither comes first.

A pair is equal however different the objects are. When a bug hits a speeding truck's windshield, the bug pushes on the truck exactly as hard as the truck pushes on the bug. The same push changes a light thing's motion a lot and a heavy thing's hardly at all, so the bug splats while the truck barely slows.

Gravity comes in pairs too: Earth pulls a falling apple down, and the apple pulls Earth up just as hard. Mass is how much matter a thing holds. Earth is so massive that the apple's pull barely moves it, so nobody sees Earth rise to meet the apple.

Why don't two equal, opposite forces cancel out? Forces cancel only when they act on the same object, like two teams pulling equally hard on one rope in a tug-of-war that goes nowhere. A force pair never cancels, because each one acts on a different object: the bat's push acts on the baseball and sends it flying, while the ball's push acts on the bat.

A girl and a boy on skates grip the two ends of a rope on smooth ice; she tugs hard, and he only holds on. Both of them slide toward each other, because by holding his end he pulls back, so the rope pulls him toward her as it pulls her toward him. The two pulls act on two different skaters, so they do not cancel.

Swimming works by a pair, too: a swimmer's hands push the water backward, and the water pushes back on her hands, forward, and that push from the water moves her along. Her arms cannot move her by pulling on her own body, since forces between the parts of one body cancel out. Nor does she store up force with each stroke: a force lasts only while two things act on each other.

A rocket's engine pushes hot gas out of the back, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. Even in airless space, a spacecraft that fires its engine speeds up, pushed forward by the gas it blasts out. A rocket never needs air to push against; it works even better in a vacuum, a space with no air, where its exhaust escapes freely. A blown-up balloon let go is a rocket you can try: the air rushing out of its neck pushes it the opposite way.

People once doubted that. In 1920 a New York Times editorial mocked the rocket pioneer Robert Goddard, claiming a rocket needed something better than a vacuum to push on. In July 1969, during the flight of Apollo 11, the paper printed a correction, saying it regretted the error.
